The town is now prepared to furnish martial music on State occasions with Judge Carson as drum major.
PRAISE God from whom all blessings flow! The cold wave has at last put in a grateful appearance.

JUDGE VARNON convened his court yesterday, but on account of the election adjourned it till this morning.

The five shares of Farmers Bank stock advertised in this paper were sold by Dr. J. G. Carpenter to Ben. Holtzclaw at $150.

The Crab Orchard Springs management gives a grand ball next Friday night in honor of its distinguished guest, Gov. Proctor Knott.

GEORGE WEST, colored, was tried before 'Squire G. P. Bright yesterday and acquitted on the charge of stealing a lot of sugar from Mr. Joe Swope.

The mob which went to Danville to hang Anderson was probably a hundred strong, but the most of them could not keep their counsel and the result was a complete failure of their plans.

MARDELLE's tent show which was on hand at the Hustonville Fair was to give a performance here yesterday, but he could not raise the $20 license required, so quietly folded his tent and stole away to more congenial climes.

News comes from Gallatin that Contractor J. C. Rodemer is pushing his work rapidly and claims that he will have everything ready for the superstructure by January 1. We would like to hear of some more of the work being let, this end for instance.

On our report of the heinous assault on Mrs. J. H. Hiatt by the negro Anderson, Mr. Hiatt complains that no reference was made to his efforts to secure the rascal. He says he was in hot pursuit of him all the afternoon and had he been with the capturing party, would have made short work of the negro

WHILE Mr. N. W. Sampson was at work in his meadow the other day he discovered a large garter snake with a brood of 79 young ones, each fully six inches in length, following her. He called all hands together and succeeded in killing all of them. Mr. Simpson says if any one doubts the truth of this statement he can prove it by five other prominent farmers living near by who were present at the time the snakes were killed and saw them counted.

A good rain, which we learn from those attending court yesterday, fell pretty generally all over the county, came Sunday and Sunday night to gladden the heart of the farmer and bring comfort to the perspiring populace. We never knew a longer hot spell than that which we hope ended with yesterday. The rain insures a good yield from most of the corn in this section, even if no more should fall soon, and should it come seasonably the farmers will have to tear down their barns and build greater ones to hold the immense crop promised.

It was reported Saturday night that there were parties here to liberate Bill Carson and kill the negro boy, Rusty Welch, had the mob got into the jail to bring out and hang the negro boys, Embry, Johnson and Hanesford, and as one piece of lawlessness begets others, the report may not have been without foundation. In this connection it may not be out of place to suggest that somebody may get hurt if they attempt to run rough-shod over Jailer Newland. He has no more sympathy with the scoundrels who assault ladies than the best man who advocates their summary punishment. But he is a conscientious man who regards his oath to protect his prisoners and defend the county's property and he does not propose to be caught napping. He is a quiet, unassuming man, who attends strictly to his own business, and does not wish to be forced to defend to the bitter end those entrusted to his safe-keeping against those he knows to be his friends.

ELECTION DAY TROUBLES.—Sam Gragg, who brutally murdered a negro with an ax, but was acquitted at the last term of the Circuit Court because of a lack of witnesses in the case, wanted to kill another negro here yesterday and drew his pistol on him for that purpose. Marshal Newland, however, prevented him and attempted to take him to jail, when he resisted in a most furious manner. Dink Farmer and one or two others of the special police came to the marshal's assistance and others to help Graggs and a general fight seemed imminent. Newland held to his man with a death grip and finally with the assistance of Sheriff Menefee landed Graggs in jail. Bill Latin attempted to interfere with Mr. Menefee and came near getting a pistol ball in his person for his trouble. Afterwards Newland and Farmer lodged George Daugherty in jail for resisting them in the discharge of their dutv. From all we can learn the fellow Gragg is a desperate character. It was told of him yesterday that when Rev. Babcock was up on Neal's creek to preach a short time ago he went to the church with an ax saying that he intended to kill him: He made no demonstrations however, but subsequently fired into a crowd of persons standing at a neighbor's house. It is to be hoped he will not get off so easily this time as in the other case, when he and his brother were the sole witnesses to the murder they committed.

The Sheriff, jailer and a couple of policemen pursued Jim Gragg yesterday evening and arrested him out in the country for resisting an officer and attempting to take his, brother Sam from the marshal. He had his pistol in his hand when overtaken but a couple of shotguns brought down on him made him drop it. He was taken be fore Judge Varnon and held in $500 bail The officers deserve much praise for the way they handled the law-breakers yesterday. That class of cattle can't take this town and they need not try.

S. J. EMBRY and W. H. Miller had a little round last night over Bobbitt, but were parted before either was hurt.

We are informed by Postmaster B. G. Alford that he has made arrangement to have a sealed pouch of mail matter sent out to his office from Louisville each night to be opened here between the hours of 7 and 8 oclock each morning. This will be of great benefit to our business men, who will heartily thank Mr. Alford for taking upon himself this additional work.

WHEN it was learned Saturday night that it was the intention of the mob to also hang the negro boys confined in jail here charged with detaining the Misses Marcum against their will, a delegation of 25 or 30 leading colored men waited on Judge Varnon and volunteered as guards for their protection, but the Judge fearing that their presence at the jail might create additional trouble, ordered Sheriff Menefee and Jailer Newland to take the prisoners away. While two of them at least are pretty mean negroes and deserve to be severely punished, we do not think theis is a case which demands mob violence, especially since they are in the hands of the law. That they were mistaken in the girls is evident, else they would not have given themselves away on their return to town by telling in the presence of an officer what they had done. Persons who compose mobs should consider well before taking the law in their hands and remember that it is as much murder for a hundred persons to kill a man as if one alone did it.

WE now receive the Louisville and Cincinnati mail that is deposited in the offices there before 8 o'clock P. M., by the night express and it is ready for delivery here at 7:30 next morning. The night mail for those and points beyond is made up here at 7 P.M. The arrangement saves one day in the transmission of mail and is a great benefit to the business men as well as others.

The right kind of a man is Deputy Collector C. M. Randall, of London. He tendered his resignation to Collector Bronston as soon as the latter took charge of the office, subject to his approval and is ready any time to give away to a democrat. He says there are a number of men in the district as capable as he of performing the duties of the office and he believes that democrats ought to be given a chance.

COUNTY COURT was held Tuesday, owing to the election on the regular day, when a great deal of business, most of it uninteresting to the general public, was transacted Mrs. Susan Stewart's will, which gives all of her property to Miss Mamie Beszley in token of her regard for her and as compensation for her love and services, was admitted to probate. J. A. Harris, William Burton and John Bright were appointed commissioners to devide the land, furniture and silverware of the estate of Roy Beszley among his heirs. The will of Mr. James Crow was also probated. It makes his sons, O. J. and C. K. Crow, the executors without security, provides for the payment of $2,500 due his wife from the sale of the property owned by her at the time of their marriage, gives her $180 per year during her life; bequeath's his Welch farm valued at $11,160 to the children by her, Mrs. Maggie McAfee and C. L. Crow and orders all his other land and personal property to be sold and proceeds to be divided equally among his five sons by his first marriage, after the amount advanced each has been deducted.

The night the mob went to Danville to hang Anderson the jailer had heard of its coming and quietly removed his prisoner to a room in the Court-house, and it was to disarm its suspicion that he so politely showed the men through the jail. The next day the negro was taken to the Harrodsburg jail and then to Lexington, where he now is.

The cowardliness of mobs in general and their inclination to commit any kind of lawlessness when ostensibly trying to aid the law, was illustrated Saturday night by a number of the fellows who went to Danville to hang the negro Anderson, stopping Addie King and Kenley Tribble, a couple of boys, who were driving along the pike. They cursed King, whom they claimed to have been after for a long time and attempted to take him from the buggy with the avowed intention of tying him to the fence. He succeeded however in getting away from them and reached home by a roundabout way. This is a beautiful way for the avengers of crime to act and shows that no good citizen should ever encourage a mob spirit. Oftener than otherwise there are men in mobs who more deserve death than the one they start out to kill.

PUTTING IT TO THEM.—Judge Carson fined Jim Gragg and George Daugherty, charged with resisting the officers on election day and attempting to take Sam Gragg from them, $50 each, the full extent of the town law for the offense. They were unable to pay or replevy and will consequently spend 50 days on the rock pile. Sam Gragg was charged with carrying a concealed weapon and drawing it on a negro man. He was brought out for trial, when he was almost stupified by having a warrant read to him charging him with stealing the pistol he had drawn and other articles to the value of $15 from a man named Mason. As this was a graver offense the Judge gave it precedence and set the examining trial for Saturday, but Gragg subsequently decided that it was best to waive an examination and he was returned to jail, unable to execute a bail bond. There seems to be no doubt about the theft of the pistol as the owner fully identified it, even to the peculiar character of a spring it contained. Besides the one so foully murdered near McKinney, the Graggs are said to have killed another negro in Kansas and one at least of them, to have served a term in the penitentiary from Pulaski in which county they are now wanted for some crime.

While Representative-elect Fontaine Fox Bobbitt was in town Tuesday, we took occasion to interview him as to his politics and accordingly asked:

"Mr. Bobbitt, it is charged that a considerable similarity exists between you and the Irishman's flea, in that it is almost as hard to place you as it is to find that nimble insect, after you catch him. What I want to know is, have you any politics to speak of and if so what is the nature of the same?"

With characteristic gestures and in his unusually ready manner, he replied:

"I answer you as I answered on a former occasion when speaking at Highland, where they are nearly all republicans, being asked that question by an enemy in the audience, who thought that I was afraid to answer, or that my answer would ruin me in a radical precinct. I said, 'Now sir, you think you have asked me a question that I am afraid to answer. I am a democrat, sir, from the crown of my head to the sole of my feet, from the centre of my system to the circumference of the same, in all my length and breadth, high and depth, width and thickness, extent and dimensions, magnitude and proderosity. I am a democrat living, I am a democrat dying, and when dead an unearthly supulchral voice from the obliquious tomb will cry out, here lies Bobbitt, the embodiment of democracy!" and the audience sent up a shout that shook the leaves of the forest," and he smole the smile of a man who seemed supremely satisfied with himself.

BLOODTHIRSTY KENTUCKY. TURN ON THE LIGHT.
Disgusting Miscarriage of Justice—The Farce of Trying White Men—A Brutal Murder Ignored by the Grand Jury—Colored Ladies Assaulted by White Ruffians—Indiana News.

Louisville, Aug. 2.—Judge W. L. Jackson and Maj. W. R. Kinney of this city, who were sent to Letcher County, by Gov. Knott, are now holding court at Whitesburg and the only cases they have tried are the Commonwealth against Samuel Holcombe, aged sixty years; William Holcombe, aged twenty, and Martin Holcombe, aged seventeen years—all being poor white men. The son of Samuel Holcombe was acquitted by the jury, and Martin was released so he could procure a new trial for his father and brother. The Holcombes are known as cut-throats and murderers, and have eluded the law of Kentucky like the Craig-Tolliver gang in Rowan County, who were also recently acquitted. Everybody who has any sense knows that the people of Kentucky have no possible way of making their wishes respected in such cases and now the miserable end of this wretched farce is seen.

The Courier-Journal promised that these men should be committed without bail. But they were discharged as innocent of all offense. Everybody knew this would be done. Squire Phillips was selected by McKenzie, the sheriff, at the instance of Young, the county attorney, to try the case, because McKenzie and Young knew that regardless of proof, Phillips would do exactly what he did do. And now the Courier Journal condemns Young, and says the people of the State condemn him. What if they do? Now, we want to give the Courier-Journal and all others who concern themselves about this matter some information. Taylor Young is a candidate for Commonwealth Attorney in that district; every Democratic partisan paper in that district sounds Young's praise for the plan he concocted to free those scoundrels. He will be nominated for his dirty work as sure as the convention is held. When nominated those who oppose him will be hounded down, black-guarded and proscribed in politics and business affairs. The Courier-Journal, following its own precedents, will receive the action of the convention as a vindication of Young and as evidence that all the charges against him are untrue, and all the chances are that it will then array itself on the side of successful scoundrelism, which it has so often done in the past.

The Southern Press still continues to harp on the Pall Mall Gazette exposure of the crimes of London. The London crimes are no comparison to the crimes committed on the colored people by the whites of the United States, especially in the Southern States. Look at the thousands of seductions; the thousands of murders; the thousands of assassinations; the thousands who have been mobbed; the thousands who have been tortured, and at the thousands who have been burnt and run away from their own homes; the millions who have been hindered and denied the protection of the laws, when their lives and families' lives were in jeopardy. Can any Southern journalist cite us to an English catalogue of crimes to equal the inhumanities and barbarities here mentioned? We need a Pall Mall Gazette in every town south of Mason and Lixon's line.

Then look at Tennessee, at Georgia, North Carolina, South Carolina, Mississippi, Louisiana, Arkansas, Texas and Maryland. London nor Paris could produce so dark a
Can the reader cite us to a General Booth or a Chas. Haddon Spurgeon in the Southern States willing to expose the crimes of their white brothers toward the colored man and woman? The wretched white press by their silence or connivance encourage the seducer, the mobber, the assassin, and the libertine. If it be a mob the white press will say: "Another culprit brought to justice," or "Judge Lynch did his duty," in such a State or town. Let us organize, and protest against these inhumanities.

In the long list of unpunished murderers in Georgia, another one goes free without even an interference of the law or the usual sham trial that white men have in that State for killing inoffensive colored men and women. A special dispatch sent to the Louisville Commercial, dated July 29, from Lincoln County, gives the details of a most horrible crime. A well-to-do farmer named Canady had a colored man employed. The man had worked for Canady six months without even drawing his pay, so says the special, to save some money. By chance one day he met a man who had worked for Canady twelve months with the same intention of accumulating money. This man said when the year was out he asked Canady for his wages. Canady put him off day after day and at last drove him off the farm. This was poor encouragement for Canady's two laborers, and both quit work and asked for the wages due them. One had worked for six months and the other for one month. Canady refused to pay them all he owed them, so they concluded to quit work unless he paid them all. Canady refused and told them if they were not satisfied with his proposition to leave his farm. The colored men left, but in a few days the one who had worked for six months returned, thinking Canady had got over his passion and would pay him. Canady cursed, swore and went into the house after his gun. When he returned the man was out of range and made good his escape. Canady is cousin to Joseph Dill, a planter who is said to be worth $10,000. Dill has two sons, Peter and David. These young savages decided to punish the runaway colored man. They induced him to meet them

by the elder Canada and the elder Dill, that the young brutes desisted, having inflicted 500 lashes. The colored man died a short time afterward, and a jury of inquest pronounced his death murder. It was fully expected when the grand jury met that some action would be taken, but the foreman of the jury was a relative of the Dills and Canadys and succeeded in getting the bill ignored, and the young brutal savages to-day go free.

Our young men will assemble in convention at Paris, Ky., Wednesday, Aug. 26, to discuss the following questions: (1) "Political parties and their relation to the country;" (2) "Do the colored people owe any obligation to the Republican party?" (3) "The present Administration, and its effect upon the country;" (4) "The benefits derived from the late civil war;" (5) "Southern outrages;" (6) "The memory and deeds of our fathers;" (7) "Have colored men any place in history?" (8) "Who saved the Union, the North or the South?" (9) "The Civil Rights bill;" (10) "The Southern Exposition at New Orleans;" (11) "The injustice of the railroads toward us as people;" (12) "Negro Democrats;" (13) "Should the colored people celebrate Emancipation Day?" (14) "Is the word 'Negro' properly used when applied to the colored people?" (15) "Has the colored race received justice according to the United States Constitution?" (16) "Is our race more immoral than others?" (17) "Colored authors, writers, lawyers and doctors;" (18) "The industrial outlook of the race;" (19) "The power of a well-trained and united people;" (20) "Should we emigrate to Africa, and if so, why?"

INDIANA ITEMS.—The colored people of Corydon commenced their camp meeting last Sunday, August 2. The attendance was the largest ever seen on the grounds. Richard Childs of New Albany was arraigned in the city court yesterday on a charge of stealing seventy-five cents in cash and a note for $73 from Mrs. Elizabeth Leppert. The defendant is an express driver and was engaged in hauling the woman to the county asylum when the theft was alleged to have taken place. The defendant was acquitted. This infamous lie was told on Mr. Childs for spite, it seems, as there was an old feud existing against Childs. The colored Post, G. A. R., of Jeffersonville, will hold a camp fi. at Oakland Garden on the 29th of August. A sham battle will be one of the features. Brutal Circus Men.
A REVOLTING OUTRAGE PERPETRATED BY A GANG OF ROUGHs.
HUNTINGDON, PA., August 11.—Ten white men and a negro named George Mack, belonging to a circus, last night committed a brutal outrage upon Flora Morrison, a pretty country girl of Center Union, this county. While the circus performance was going on she was taken into the woods near the show grounds and assaulted by the men. J. K. McCahn, in trying to rescue the girl, was severely clubbed by the negro. The girl was taken to a neighboring house for safety. The negro was captured and consigned to jail.
george-mock-huntingdon-1885-08-10.A3:
ASSAULTED BY TWELVE MEN.
HUNTINGDON, Pa., Aug. 11.—Bertha Morrison, aged 17, a modest and attractive young woman, lives with her widowed mother at Centre Union, in this county. Miss Morrison, accompanied by a number of her young friends, started early last evening for the grounds where Cole's circus was exhibiting. By some means she become separated from her associates in the crowd. While trying to find them she was approached by a stylishly dressed young man named Kimberlain, alias "Fatty," of Altoona, who proposed that they go into the show. Miss Morrison at first objected, but after repeated persuasions consented to accompany him. Instead of taking her to the circus, however, Kimberlain enticed her to walk around the tents, and after getting her beyond the hearing of the people who had congregated at the entrance, eleven other attachés of the circus, including two colored men, emerged suddenly from their concealment in the bushes, and grasping the struggling girl, gagged her and carried her across several fields into the woods, where they repeatedly assaulted her. Her garments were torn into shreds, and her face, arms, and body were shockingly bruised.

At last, when there was no one with the girl except the negroes, her piteous cries for assistance were heard by John McCohen, a neighbor who was passing. Hastening to her assistance, McCohen drove the negroes away, and, after carrying the girl to a house, started to notify the police. The negroes were lying in wait, and beat him until he was insensible. The police were notified, and after searching the circus train which was about starting for Bedford, they succeeded in arresting only one of the guilty men. George Mock, colored, who was found secreted, in a carriage. He was arraigned before Justice Murray this afternoon, and, upon being identified by his victim, was remanded to jail. Officers will leave at once for Bedford to arrest the other participants in the crime. There is strong talk of lynching Mock.
george-mock-huntingdon-1885-08-10.A4:
BEATEN WITH A CLUB BY A NEGRO.
HUNTINGDON, Penn., Aug. 11.—Last night after the performance at Cole's circus a young girl named Flora Morrison, from near Centre Union, in this county, was enticed by a showman into a thicket near the grounds, where she was assaulted by him and other men. "Jack" McCahan, who was on his way from the show to his home near by, heard the screams of the girl, and going to her rescue protected her from a powerful colored man. McCahan was about to take her home with him when her assailant followed. He was warned to desist from the pursuit, McCahan exhibiting a pistol and threatening to use it. The negro dared him to shoot, which unfortunately he could not do as the pistol was not loaded. Turning toward his home and with his back to the angry black man, he was struck over the head from behind with a heavy club and throwing up his arms to protect himself he was beaten until he was insonsible and his hands were rendered powerless. He fell into a stream of water, where he remained until consciousness returned. By this time the circus train was standing on the railroad track ready to start for Bedford. Policeman Decker and others searched the train and found a man who answered to the description of McCahan's assailant lying as if concealed under the canvas that covered the steam callows. He was taken into custody, but neither McCahan nor Miss Morrison could positively identify him. To-day at the hearing, however, a witness appeared who testified that he saw the assault on the girl, that the prisoner was one of the man, that he ran to get somebody to help him save the girl, and that before he returned McCahan had appeared and the assault on him had occurred. george-mock-huntingdon-1885-08-10.A11:
Another Miscreant Captured.
HUNTINGDON, Pa., Aug. 14. —John, alias "Fatty." Kimberlin, notorious as a desperado and villain of the deepest dye, was arrested in Altoona Wednesday afternoon, brought here late in the night and lodged in jail. He is known as the principal in the brutal outrage of the unfortunate Miss Morrison near the show grounds on Monday night. He had formed a conspiracy with eleven attaches of Cole's circus to place the girl in their power. The details of the crime become more terrible as they are more fully disclosed. The victim, who is still in a precarious condition, cannot tell the number of men to whose cruel treatment she was subjected. Excitement is intense, and extra precautions are being taken to shield too two participants, now in jail, from mob violence, which is loudly threatened.

NOTES AND COMMENTS.
Rev. George W. Bryant, pastor of the A. M. E. Church in Frankfort, Ky., was appointed the other day by President Cleveland Minister to Liberia, and he respectfully declined. Rev. Bryant is an earnest Republican.

Editor Bailey and Manager Fulton, of the Little Rock Sun, were arrested last week, charged with libel on account of the article "Southland College and its Management," which appeared in the Sun a few weeks ago.

W. A. Cole, the circus owner, has bought J. A. Bailey's interest in the Barnum show. Bailey's health is shattered. He retires with a fortune of $2,000,000 as the result of five years with Barnum. Cole has made a great deal of money in the circus business in Australia and California. He is said to own $1,000,000 worth of real estate in Chicago.

Twelve attaches of Cole's circus, two colored, outraged Bertha Morrison in the woods near Huntington, Pa., Monday night. John McKeon, who tried to rescue her, was nearly killed. The girl has identified colored George Mock and a lynching is imminent. The others escaped. The girl is in an awful condition.

Jeff Phillips, colored, was shot and killed Tuesday afternoon by Charles Boughner. Deputy Marshal of Chester, a suburb of Maysville, Ky. The shooting occurred on the river shore in Chester. Boughner was trying to arrest Phillips and two other Negroes for some trifling offense. They resisted and beat him over the head and drove him away. He then armed himself and overtook them. Two of them submitted, but Phillips shot at him, whereupon the Marshal fired on him.

LET others follow where they will, but let the colored man maintain his manhood, prove his devotion and consistency to right principles and forget not now the party which befriended him, defended him and raised him to the dignity of an American citizen.—CLEVELAND GAZETTE.

Right, my brother, but then there are some of our colored brothers who curse the hand that fed them.—Richmond Enterprise.
george-mock-huntingdon-1885-08-10.A19:
One of the Outrager.s
HUNTINGDON, Aug 14 — Policeman Decker and an assistant have been in pursuit of Cole's sircus since the fiendish outrage was committed upon Miss Morrison by its attaches on Monday night, with warrants on which to take anyone whom they found reason to believe guilty. They came up with it to-day at Meyersdale, Somerset county, and arrested a man who gave his name as Henry Wilson whose business with the show was to sell umbrellas at the main entrance. He was brought here this evening and put in jail. No others could be found against whom there is any strong suspicion. It is believed that several, if not all, the guilty ones have left the show until it leaves the State, which will be to-night. The outrage is still the cause of great public indignation and excitement.

Milton C. Schott, aged eight months, son of Emil Schott, of this place, died of cholera infantum, on Thursday morning. Interment at Reading, Pa., on Sunday afternoon.

The Democratic county committee met in the Court House, on Saturday, and selected Sheriff Shivery and Dr. Salm, to represent the Democracy of Juniata in the State Convention.

The Democracy of Ohio do not propose to let their bitters go, without a vigorous protest, and therefore, they have inserted a plank in their present campaign platform against prohibition.

The mugwumps insist on getting in, and it is seriously feared by the high priests of the erring brethren that the circle of the faithful cannot be kept small and select.—Forward mugwumps.

Kreps, railroad track foreman, who had been tied to a rail of the railroad track some days ago, visited Dr. D. M. Crawford's office last Friday morning to have his wounded hand dressed.

David Yeater, of Fermanagh township, has learned that his brother John Yeater, who he has not seen in sixty years lives in Indianapolis, Indiana. The brothers will soon meet each other.

The Grand Lodge of the Knights of Pythias, met at Reading, last week. Over three hundred delegates were present, there are three hundred and six lodges in the state, with a membership of 34,609.

Almost every family in East Waterford is afflicted with malaria. It is believed that a pond of stagnant water near the town generates the disease and it has been proposed to drain the pond, or fill it with dirt.

Miss Minnie McAlister, who lay sick at her father's house in McAlisterville, was brought to this place, to the home of her uncle, Mr. Hutchinson McAlister, one day last week, and is now rapidly improving in health.

Miss Gerty Jackman, Miss Carrie Derr, and Miss Ella K. Banks, after a protracted visit to Perry county friends, returned last Thursday, bringing with them the Misses Mortimer, daughters of the editor of the Bloomfield Times.

There is a beautiful Sulphur spring near McCoysville, and people in want or in need of recreation might find a pleasant day or two of it by going to McCoytown, either by taking their own conveyance or by going in Allen's stage.

Do you wish a beautiful complexion? Then use Ayer's Sarsaparilla. It cleanses and purifies the blood, and thereby removes blotches and pimples from the skin making it smooth and clear, and giving it a bright and healthy appearance.

J. F. McDonald, who has been connected with the publication of the Tribune, in this place the past year, has withdrawn from the responsible management of the paper. T. D. Garman will continue the publication and management of the paper.

The school board of Fermanagh township selected the following teachers: Cuba School, Anna G. Colyer; Arch Rock, G. L. Hower; Mount Hope, J. C. Hower; Big Run, Harry Sweigart; Happy Hollow, James A. Banks; Renno's, John Stoner.

The Presbyterian congregation of this place by a showing of hand vote, authorized the trustees and elders of the congregation to meet, on this, Wednesday evening, to consider the question of the purchase of a lot of ground on which to erect a meeting house.

Mrs. Catharine, wife of Rev. Samuel Meyers, late of Fayette township, deceased, died at the home of her son Simon Shellenberger, near McAlisterville, on the 20th inst. Interment in the Sheilenberger graveyard at Goodwill, Fayette township. Mrs. Meyers was aged 81 years.

On last Thursday afternoon, a party of young folks from this town and vicinity picniced at the Mountain View House, at Academia, kept by Dr. Brazee. The party spent the afternoon pleasantly, and after partaking of supper, passed the hours of the evening and early night in "tripping the light fantastic toe."

There is a good deal of quiet excitement in Huntingdon over the arrest and imprisonment of "Fatty Kemberling," and George Mack, colored, on the charge of violating the person of Miss Bertha Morrison on a circus day not long since. They will be tried at September term of court.

"What are the prospects in this town for a circus?" asked the advance agent of a Kentucky citizen. "Think we'd draw a crowd?" The citizen shook his head dubiously. "I'm afraid not, stranger," he said. "Thar's to be a man hung here in September, an' I reckon everybody'll be saving up money for that."

Last Thursday morning, James C. Longwell, who learned the printing trade in the office of the JUNIATA SENTINEL, thirty years ago, when under the management of of A. J. Greer, of Altoona, died suddenly of congestion of the lungs, in the office of the Scotdale, Westmoreland county, Tribune. Longwell was a native of Mifflin county. He was aged forty-seven years. He permitted himself to become the victim of habits that did only himself injury. He had been a soldier in the eleventh Pennsylvania Regiment, and his funeral took place under the management of a G. A. R. Post.

The investigation to discover the cause of the explosion on board of the S. M. Fulton, a Pennsylvania R. R. steamer that plies between Philadelphia and Wilmington, is still going on. The Fulton was just starting from the wharf at the explosion took place. About thirteen people of one hundred and ninety passengers were hurt. KEMBERLING'S BRUTAL ACCOMPLICES.
HUNTERDON Pean Sept. 3 (Special).
HUNTINGDON, Penn., Sept. 3 (Special). — "Fatty" Kemberling, the circus man who decoyed Miss Bertha Morrison into the thicket where she was assaulted by himself and ten or twelve other men, when Cole's Circus was here, and who is now in jail for his crime, has given the names of some of his accomplices. As the result of facts developed by him Samuel Stair, a young man living in Smithfield, across the river from this city, was arrested last night. The police say that they have conclusive evidence against him. Kemberling says that others now travelling with the show in Virginia are also guilty.
